transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-10-08 15:30 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Nora Patel (ArborAI - Platform Eng), Samir Khanna (ArborAI - ML Infra), Ben Turner (ArborAI - CTO)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time, we're excited to dig into the scheduling and throughput tuning. I think Luis will lead the technical part.
[00:22] Luis (Redwood SE): hi all, quick agenda: (1) current ArborAI workload shape and constraints from Nora, (2) overview of continuous batching and scheduler knobs, (3) live examples with max_num_seqs and token caps, (4) KV cache warm vs cold impacts and quantization notes, (5) next steps.
[00:40] Nora (ArborAI): sounds good. quick context — we run a multi-tenant inference cluster in our VPC, about 8 GPUs, mostly A100s. Bursty traffic, peaky hours. Each tenant has different SLAs; some low-latency chat, some bulk embeddings. We're trying to squeeze more throughput without impacting the latency SLO for priority tenants.
[01:05] Ben (CTO): also cost is a focus; if we can consolidate more workloads on the same capacity by tuning, that helps our internal chargebacks.
[01:18] Samir (ML Infra): we already tried bumping batch_size but saw tail latency spikes during bursts. Curious how continuous batching and max_num_seqs help.
[01:30] Luis: great. high-level: continuous batching keeps small requests queued briefly to fill a batch window and amortize GPU work. The scheduler has knobs: batch_window_ms, max_batch_tokens, max_num_seqs, slot_size, and backpressure thresholds. They interact — changing one without the others can push latency or OOM.
[02:05] Luis: max_num_seqs is essentially the per-device concurrency limit for sequences in flight. Think of it as how many active KV sessions / sequences we let run simultaneously. Setting it too high fragments GPU memory and KV cache, setting it too low underutilizes the GPU.
[02:30] Nora: can you give an example? say we have a lot of small chat messages, 8 tokens typical, versus some long completions 1k tokens.
[02:42] Luis: yes — for small chat, continuous batching with a low batch_window_ms (like 5-20ms) plus a higher max_num_seqs (12-24) can saturate throughput while keeping p95 latency under control. But for long requests, you need token-aware limits: a max_tokens_per_request or max_batch_tokens so the long seq doesn't fill GPU for extended time.
[03:06] Maya: important note — we expose a per-tenant token cap to avoid a single tenant blocking the scheduler. That's one of the token caps we recommend.
[03:20] Samir: is that enforced at the router or the device? we run private.
[03:26] Luis: we usually enforce at the front-end router in the private control plane, with soft and hard caps. Soft caps queue and apply QoS; hard caps reject. For on-prem/VPC, you can choose to enforce at the gateway or locally in the runtime. There's a tradeoff for immediate rejection vs slower backpressure.
[03:50] Nora: about KV cache — we saw big perf delta when the model cache warmed, like 20-30% throughput improvement. How does the scheduler account for cold-kv scenarios?
[04:06] Luis: cold KV cache means large memory churn and more GPU work per request. A few approaches: (1) preferential scheduling: keep hot tenants on pinned devices (device affinity), (2) ramping max_num_seqs during warmup, (3) pre-warming via synthetic requests or dedicated warm-up background jobs. You can also set a higher slot_size temporarily to reduce context switches while cache warms.
[04:42] Nora: is pre-warming safe in multi-tenant? we worry about cost and noisy-neighbor effects.
[04:50] Luis: it's safe if you use low-priority background slots and limit token budget; the runtime has a 'warmup' QoS class. But the thing to watch: warmup requests still affect memory and KV eviction policy, so you need to coordinate.
[05:10] Ben: what's the typical starting default you recommend? We're onboarding several tenants next month.
[05:18] Luis: for multi-tenant on 8xA100 with mixed short and long, we recommend default: max_num_seqs=16, batch_window_ms=12, max_batch_tokens=32768, per-tenant token_cap 200k tokens/day (soft), slot_size=1k tokens. These are conservative; we'll tune from profiles.
[05:45] Samir: curious about scheduler backpressure — we saw queue pileups and then a cascade where latency spikes.
[05:52] Luis: that's classic — if backpressure thresholds are too late, requests stack up then the runtime tries to flush giant batches. Two mitigations: (a) lower the early backpressure threshold (start shedding or queuing earlier), (b) implement token-aware admission where long requests reserve slots; short requests can be preferred via priority queues.
[06:20] Nora: token-aware admission — can that be pinned per route? we have endpoints used only for short chat.
[06:27] Luis: yes, per-route QoS is important. You can have small-window low-latency routes (batch_window_ms=8, max_num_seqs smaller) and a separate heavy-compute route with higher batch windows. The router maps route -> scheduler profile.
[06:46] Ben: about quantization — if we go int8 or int4, how does that change the knobs? we saw some degradation in quality for rare tenants.
[06:58] Luis: quantization decreases memory and compute cost, letting you increase concurrency (higher max_num_seqs) safely. But quantization may increase per-token latency slightly due to dequant/quant ops and occasionally produce quality regressions on certain prompts. A hybrid approach: run int8 for general traffic, reserve fp16 or int8-fine-tuned variants for high-quality tenants. Also, measure token-per-USD tradeoffs.
[07:35] Nora: can we have per-tenant model variant selection — e.g., tenant A uses quantized model, tenant B uses fp16?
[07:42] Luis: yes — smart routing can send requests to different model variants; the scheduler respects variant resource profiles. When capacity constrained, we can fallback to cheaper variants per policy.
[07:56] Samir: walk us through a sample profiling run we should do on-prem to get concrete numbers.
[08:02] Luis: recommended profile:
- Step 1: collect 24 hours of traffic shape (seq lengths histogram, tokens per request, arrival rates)
- Step 2: run synthetic replay for key tenants at ramped loads: 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% of current peak; include cold-start runs to capture KV warm behavior
- Step 3: enable tracing for scheduler events: batch flush times, queue lengths, per-device mem usage, KV eviction metrics
- Step 4: try a matrix of max_num_seqs (8, 16, 24) and batch_window_ms (8, 12, 20) and record p50/p95/p99 latency and throughput tokens/sec

[09:20] Nora: if we only have time for one short run, what should we set?
[09:25] Luis: run at 50% of peak with cold reload to observe warmup dynamics and try max_num_seqs=16 as a baseline.
[09:34] Ben: how do multi-tenant fairness policies work? we want to prioritize paying customers during bursts but not starve lower tiers.
[09:43] Luis: use weighted fair-share with borrowing limits. Each tenant has a weight and a max_burst_tokens. During low utilization, lower-tier tenants can borrow unused capacity. During bursts, weights decide share; hard caps prevent starvation. Also 'graceful degradation' policies let you reduce model size (fallback) before rejecting.
[10:10] Nora: any gotchas for VPC/on-prem? we use strict egress rules and HSM for KMS.
[10:18] Luis: common gaps: telemetry endpoints blocked by VPC rules — that prevents profile collection. Also, KMS latency in on-prem integration can add 10s of ms if not colocated. For private deployments, we recommend a dedicated monitoring lane that can ship anonymized metrics out-of-band, or offline log collection.
[10:42] Samir: about KMS — can we cache decrypted keys to avoid repeated KMS roundtrips?
[10:47] Luis: yes, runtime supports a short-lived key cache with strict TTL; ensure it fits your security posture. For HSM-backed keys, some customers do a local KMS proxy to reduce latency while preserving audit.
[11:05] Ben: let's get into a concrete scenario: three tenants — chat (short 8-30 tokens), batch embedding (500-1k tokens), and long-form summarization (1k-2k tokens). How to set defaults?
[11:20] Luis: design per-route profiles:
- chat-route: batch_window_ms=8, max_num_seqs=24, max_tokens_per_request=256, priority high
- embeddings-route: batch_window_ms=30, max_num_seqs=8, max_batch_tokens=65536, priority medium
- longform-route: batch_window_ms=50, max_num_seqs=4, max_tokens_per_request=2048, priority low, prefer reserved slots
This keeps chat responsive, embeddings maximize throughput, longform doesn't crowd short jobs.
[12:05] Nora: the chat-route suggestion of max_num_seqs=24 seems high — won't that blow memory?
[12:10] Luis: it depends on model size and quantization. On int8 13B models it's usually safe on A100 with 80GB; for FP16 you might need lower. That's why profiling is critical.
[12:22] Samir: what about slot_size? I saw docs mention slot_size=1024 tokens by default. Is that chunking of KV?
[12:30] Luis: slot_size is the token chunk the runtime uses to schedule and place caches. Smaller slot_size increases scheduling overhead; larger reduces flexibility. The sweet spot is often 512-1024 for mixed loads.
[12:45] Nora: we have a tenant that runs bursts of many short requests — can we throttle them without rejecting?
[12:51] Luis: yes — soft token caps with queue prioritization are ideal. You can set per-tenant rate limits and token budgets; when exceeded, lower-priority requests are delayed or routed to a cheaper quantized variant.
[13:10] Ben: let's talk about continuous batching details — is batching time-based or event-based?
[13:16] Luis: both. We use hybrid: batch_window_ms governs time-based aggregation; max_batch_tokens and max_num_seqs provide size bounds (event-based). Also we have a 'fill factor' heuristic that will flush earlier if expected latency SLO is at risk.
[13:35] Nora: any improvements for burst handling — sudden spike to 2x within seconds?
[13:40] Luis: for bursts, use burst_buckets and token borrowing. Also, configure an aggressive early-shed policy for very long requests so the short ones don't get stuck. You can also enable fast-path queues for authenticated premium tenants.
[14:00] Samir: can we tune garbage collection / KV eviction policy? we noticed frequent evictions during peaks.
[14:08] Luis: yes — eviction policy and cache size are critical. For multi-tenant, use per-tenant cache quotas to avoid thrash. LRU works but for sequence models you might want an MRU or weighted LRU that favors recently active tenants. Also monitor KV hit rate metrics and correlate with payloads.
[14:35] Nora: how are these metrics surfaced in the console? we use the Redwood Console but it's behind our firewall in private deployment.
[14:42] Luis: Console for private has a collector agent that ships metrics to your internal Grafana; we also provide an optional read-only snapshot export you can import. For strict air-gapped, we produce self-contained bundles.
[14:58] Ben: curious about admission control when model variants differ in memory footprint — how does scheduler account?
[15:05] Luis: each variant advertises resource profile (mem, seq_overhead, token_throughput). Scheduler uses that to binpack requests per-device. Admission considers both active mem reservations and expected peak mem during generation. That's why token-aware admission helps: long tokens reserve more mem.
[15:28] Nora: what's the expected p95 impact when switching from fp16 to int8 for similar concurrency?
[15:34] Luis: typical observation: throughput increases 20-50%, memory drops significantly, p50 often improves, but p95 can be slightly worse for some patterns due to additional dequant work and cache pressure. Again, run A/B testing on customer prompts.
[15:55] Samir: any guardrails you recommend to prevent misconfiguration causing OOM?
[16:00] Luis: start with conservative max_num_seqs and monitor per-device memory headroom. Enable predictive OOM checks which simulate reservation before admitting, and set an OOM margin of 5-10% to avoid surprises. Also limit per-request max_tokens hard.
[16:20] Nora: earlier you mentioned slot preallocation during warmup — can you expand?
[16:25] Luis: during warmup we can preallocate slots and KV entries for expected hot keys; it's like prefetching. It costs memory transiently but reduces churn. Use it for tenants with predictable patterns.
[16:40] Ben: what about horizontal scaling vs higher concurrency — should we add more devices or push max_num_seqs?
[16:48] Luis: both have tradeoffs: increasing concurrency (max_num_seqs) is cheaper but risks higher tail latency and cache thrash. Horizontal scaling adds capacity isolation at cost. Typically start with conservative concurrency tuning and benchmark; if you still need more steady throughput, add devices.
[17:05] Nora: do you support tenant isolation via node pinning?
[17:08] Luis: yes — device affinity / pinning is supported; dedicated pools reduce noisy neighbor risk but reduce binpacking efficiency. A hybrid approach: pin highest-paying tenants and binpack the rest.
[17:25] Samir: we want to try a quick experiment: run two configs and compare. Can you propose the two config diffs?
[17:31] Luis: propose A (latency-first): max_num_seqs=12, batch_window_ms=8, token_cap per tenant soft 150k/day; B (throughput-first): max_num_seqs=24, batch_window_ms=20, token_cap per tenant soft 300k/day, with int8 quantization. We'll supply the exact YAML diffs.
[17:55] Nora: will the runtime automatically re-balance when we flip configs?
[18:00] Luis: yes — rolling rollout with canary is supported; you can apply config per pool. We recommend canary with 10% of traffic for 24-48 hours then expand.
[18:12] Ben: any concerns about data residency or logs when doing the profiling?
[18:18] Maya: we can limit telemetry to anonymized metrics — no PII. For on-prem we can also keep logs local and transfer a redacted bundle. We'll include our security checklist in the follow-up.
[18:35] Nora: ok let's talk about automatic fallback to cheaper variants under load — how smooth is that?
[18:40] Luis: fallback is policy-driven: you can define steps (fp16 -> int8 -> distilled) and thresholds. The router will transparently remap requests; we recommend instrumenting a lightweight QA check so critical tenants can veto fallback for sensitive prompts.
[19:05] Samir: are there APIs to programmatically adjust token caps per tenant?
[19:10] Luis: yes — admin APIs allow token budgets, weights, and per-route profiles. They integrate with your billing system.
[19:18] Nora: when a tenant reaches soft cap and is queued, do we get hooks to notify them?
[19:24] Luis: webhook hooks exist; you can notify and give a grace period. Also rate limiting headers are returned in responses for SDKs.
[19:35] Ben: let's cover an observed failure mode: we had a situation where a single long request stalled the whole device for >30s and caused p99 spikes. Diagnostics?
[19:44] Luis: check admission logs — see if long requests reserved memory without preemption. Fixes: enable preemptive slot eviction for long jobs, shorter per-request token hard cap, and route long requests to dedicated low-priority slots. Also review max_batch_tokens so a single long request can't fill a batch.
[20:10] Nora: can the scheduler preempt half-done generations?
[20:16] Luis: preemption mid-generation is tricky and can leave partial outputs; we prefer to avoid mid-token preemption. Instead, preempt at sequence boundaries or limit admission so it doesn't happen. For streaming flows, you can reduce chunk sizes.
[20:35] Samir: any notable mis-transcriptions we should be careful of in logs (funny but real)?
[20:40] Luis: haha logs sometimes say "kv cash" or "max num sex" when the speech model messes up. we've seen that.
[20:50] Nora: thanks. back to benchmarks — what metrics should we record to compare config A vs B?
[20:56] Luis: collect: tokens/sec, GPU utilization, per-device memory headroom, p50/p95/p99 latencies for key routes, KV hit rate, batch sizes distribution, queue length percentiles, and error/reject rates.
[21:20] Ben: sample size? how long should we run each canary?
[21:25] Luis: 24-72 hours is good to capture diurnal patterns; for quick checks 4 hours at peak is ok.
[21:35] Nora: about tooling — any scripts to export scheduler traces?
[21:40] Luis: yes — we have a trace exporter that outputs CSVs and flamegraphs. We'll send the link.
[21:48] Maya: we'll attach the scheduler knobs doc and a benchmark template after the call.
[22:00] Samir: question on eviction policies: is there a way to prefer evicting older long sequences instead of recently used short ones?
[22:08] Luis: yes — weighted eviction with per-tenant and per-route weights; favor keeping recent short-chat keys.
[22:20] Nora: do you have any examples of customers who doubled throughput via tuning rather than adding hardware?
[22:25] Luis: yes, one customer shifted to int8, tuned batch_window and max_num_seqs and saw 1.8x tokens/sec with similar p95. We'll anonymize and share the case study.
[22:40] Ben: operationally, if we adopt these recommendations, what's the risk window? will we risk regressions?
[22:48] Luis: risk exists, but can be controlled: canary, telemetry, automatic rollback on defined QoS regression. Also keep a shadow fleet so you can compare A/B without user impact.
[23:05] Nora: one last thing — do we have guardrails for per-tenant billing when token caps are hit and fallback occurs? we don't want surprises.
[23:13] Maya: billing hooks and alerts are supported; you can set notice thresholds and automatic rate-limit escalations.
[23:25] Ben: thanks. let's recap and next steps.
[23:30] Maya: recap: Redwood to share scheduler knobs doc, YAML diffs for config A and B, benchmark template, and security checklist. Customer to run profiling (50% peak cold-run + 100% peak test) and grant ephemeral telemetry. Follow-up 2025-10-15 to review.
[23:52] All: thanks.
[24:00] (end of recorded transcript)

Notes about transcript quality: some words were garbled by the recorder (e.g., "kv cash" instead of KV cache, "max num sex" for max_num_seqs). We kept filler words and interruptions to preserve authenticity.
